scenes.heading: UK Compliance Landscape
scenes.subheading: Who regulates what, and why it shapes every client's compliance year
scenes.narration: Welcome to Module 1. This is the regulator map every UK accountant must hold in their head, not as trivia, but as the operating system every client's compliance year runs on.

scenes.heading: Tuesday: a new café client
scenes.narration: Picture a one-shop café owner who signs your engagement letter and wants to incorporate next quarter. You haven't done any work yet, but obligations are already in motion.

items.label: Engagement letter signed
items.detail: A one-shop café owner becomes your client

items.label: Incorporating soon
items.detail: The owner plans to incorporate next quarter

items.label: No work done yet
items.detail: Yet several regulators already expect action

scenes.heading: Who wants what from the café
scenes.narration: HM Revenue and Customs wants VAT returns through Making Tax Digital, payroll submissions and a corporation tax return. Companies House, the Information Commissioner's Office and the Pensions Regulator each have duties too.

items.label: HMRC
items.detail: VAT via MTD, EPS on payroll, CT600 within 12 months

items.label: Companies House
items.detail: Annual confirmation statement, accounts, PSC register

items.label: ICO
items.detail: Data-protection fee paid before taking card payments

items.label: The Pensions Regulator
items.detail: Auto-enrolment duties from the first hire

scenes.heading: Who supervises the accountant
scenes.narration: Your professional body, such as ACCA, ICAEW, CIOT, AAT, ICB or IFA, supervises your anti-money laundering compliance and continuing professional development. And OPBAS supervises those bodies.

items.label: You, the accountant
items.detail: Must meet AML and CPD duties

items.label: Your professional body
items.detail: ACCA, ICAEW, CIOT, AAT, ICB or IFA supervises you

items.label: OPBAS
items.detail: Supervises the professional bodies

scenes.heading: What happens if you slip
scenes.narration: Miss a deadline and an automatic penalty starts, with no court order and no warning. Skip anti-money laundering supervision entirely and it's a criminal offence under the Money Laundering Regulations 2017.

items.label: Missed deadline
items.detail: Penalty starts with no court order and no warning

items.label: No AML supervision
items.detail: Criminal offence under MLR 2017, up to two years inside

scenes.heading: What this module covers
scenes.narration: In this module we'll map each regulator, what it demands and when, how supervision of accountants works, and the penalties that follow if anything is missed.

scenes.heading: UK Business Structures
scenes.subheading: Sole trader or Ltd? Why the right structure matters from day one
scenes.narration: Every accountant hears it: sole trader or limited company? The honest answer is never a one-liner, and in this module we'll learn how to answer it well.

scenes.heading: What the choice depends on
scenes.narration: The right structure depends on five things: the profit profile, liability exposure, growth plan, exit intent, and how the owner wants to take cash out.

items.label: Profit profile
items.detail: How much the business earns

items.label: Liability exposure
items.detail: Risk of being sued

items.label: Growth and exit
items.detail: Plans to grow or sell

items.label: Cash extraction
items.detail: How the owner takes money out

scenes.heading: Two builders, £80k profit each
scenes.narration: Two builders with identical eighty thousand pound profits can rationally choose differently. One values simplicity, the other values limited liability, credibility and an easier sale.

items.label: Stays sole trader
items.detail: Simpler; full Class 4 NI; unlimited liability accepted

items.label: Incorporates as Ltd
items.detail: Slightly lower tax; limited liability; easier exit

scenes.heading: The wrong choice compounds
scenes.narration: Getting it wrong costs real money year after year. Overpaying fifteen hundred pounds in admin, or four thousand in tax, adds up to fifteen or forty thousand pounds over a decade.

items.label: Unneeded Ltd admin
items.detail: £1.5k a year in fees over a decade

items.label: Missed Ltd tax saving
items.detail: £4k a year in extra tax over a decade

scenes.heading: CIC or charity?
scenes.narration: The same applies to social enterprises. A charity can unlock Gift Aid and rate relief, while a Community Interest Company can allow dividends to fund the founders.

items.label: Charity
items.detail: Can unlock Gift Aid and rate relief

items.label: CIC
items.detail: Can allow dividends to fund founders

scenes.heading: The seven-structure map
scenes.narration: We'll map seven structures, comparing legal personality, liability, tax regime, public disclosure and governance documents, so every later decision sits on a sound foundation.

scenes.heading: Double-Entry from First Principles
scenes.subheading: The bedrock system every UK small business's books still run on
scenes.narration: Welcome to Bookkeeping Fundamentals. Double-entry is the system every UK small and medium business still runs on, and every later module builds on it.

scenes.heading: Old Logic, Still Unchanged
scenes.narration: In 1494, the Italian friar Luca Pacioli codified double-entry in a section of a 600-page maths book. The logic hasn't changed in 530 years.

items.label: Pacioli codifies the system
items.detail: In Summa de Arithmetica, part of a 600-page maths book

items.label: Years the logic has held
items.detail: Still the basis of every set of books today

scenes.heading: The Three Core Rules
scenes.narration: Every transaction touches at least two accounts, debits always equal credits, and assets equal liabilities plus equity after every single posting.

items.label: Two accounts at least
items.detail: Every transaction touches two or more accounts

items.label: Debits equal credits
items.detail: Both sides always balance

items.label: The accounting equation
items.detail: Assets = Liabilities + Equity, after every posting

scenes.heading: What Software Hides
scenes.narration: Xero shows you a bank reconciliation and QuickBooks shows you a sales invoice, but underneath, every single line is still a debit and a credit.

items.label: On screen
items.detail: A bank reconciliation in Xero, a sales invoice in QuickBooks

items.label: Underneath
items.detail: Every single line is still a debit and a credit

scenes.heading: Eight Patterns, Post Anything
scenes.narration: Learn the eight universal transaction patterns and you can post anything, rather than copy-pasting from Google. And yes, sales returns are a debit.

items.label: Wage and tax accruals
items.detail: Including a year-end corporation tax provision

scenes.heading: What This Module Covers
scenes.narration: We'll cover the equation, the five account types, the eight patterns and the trial balance, including what it critically doesn't detect. Master this and later modules like FRS 102 come far easier.

scenes.subheading: The backbone of every accounting system: every posting lands in one of its accounts
scenes.narration: Welcome to Module 4. The chart of accounts is the backbone of every accounting system, because every single posting lands in one of its accounts.

scenes.heading: What the structure determines
scenes.narration: The structure of the chart of accounts decides whether you can produce four things: a clean profit and loss, a compliant balance sheet, a VAT return that ties out, and readable management accounts.

items.label: VAT return

scenes.narration: Done well, the chart of accounts is invisible and numbers flow into reports. Done badly, every month-end is a puzzle and year-end reclassification can take three days.

items.label: Done badly

scenes.heading: The Bookkeeping Cycle
scenes.subheading: From source document to trial balance: the nine-step monthly close
scenes.narration: Welcome to Module 5. What separates a bookkeeper who closes the month in two working days from one still chasing reconciliations a fortnight later isn't speed. It's the cycle.

scenes.heading: The 5th of the Month
scenes.narration: Picture it: last month's books need closing, and on your desk sit hundreds of invoices, expense claims, bank transactions, two payroll runs and a VAT return due in three weeks.

items.label: Supplier invoices
items.detail: Waiting to be processed

items.label: Expense claims
items.detail: Plus a director's coffee receipt

items.label: Bank transactions
items.detail: On one bank statement

items.label: VAT return due
items.detail: Alongside two payroll runs

scenes.heading: The Nine-Step Cycle
scenes.narration: The cycle is a defined nine-step sequence, run the same way every month with controls at each step: capture, code, post, bank rec, control accounts, adjusting journals, trial balance, review and lock.

items.label: Capture, code, post
items.detail: Steps 1 to 3: get documents into the books

items.label: Bank rec, control accounts
items.detail: Steps 4 and 5: reconcile and check

items.label: Adjusting journals
items.detail: Step 6: correct and adjust

items.label: Trial balance
items.detail: Step 7: the natural output of steps 1 to 6

items.label: Review and lock
items.detail: Steps 8 and 9: check and close the period

scenes.heading: Skip a Step, Errors Compound
scenes.narration: Skip a step or do them out of order and errors compound. A missed bank rec hides duplicates, an unreconciled VAT control builds a misstatement, and a skipped review misses margin drift for a quarter.

items.label: Missed bank rec
items.detail: Duplicate invoices stay hidden

items.label: Unreconciled VAT control
items.detail: Misstatement silently builds up

items.label: No analytical review
items.detail: Gross-margin drift unnoticed for a quarter

scenes.heading: Two Ways to Close the Month
scenes.narration: The difference isn't working faster. Run the cycle properly and you can close in two working days; without it, you could still be chasing reconciliations a fortnight later.

items.label: Running the cycle
items.detail: Same sequence monthly, controls at each step

items.label: No defined cycle
items.detail: Still chasing reconciliations

scenes.heading: What This Module Covers
scenes.narration: In this module we'll cover the nine-step monthly close, the controls at each step, and the bank reconciliation discipline that catches the issues every other step misses.

scenes.heading: Source Documents & Record-Keeping
scenes.subheading: Why you must be able to produce records now, not just once have had them
scenes.narration: Welcome to Module 6. Keeping source documents isn't just tidy admin: the penalty regime cares whether you can produce your records now, not whether you had good books once.

scenes.heading: The Schedule 36 Notice
scenes.narration: Picture this. Three years after a clean year-end, a client gets a Schedule 36 information notice from HMRC, and the enquiry officer wants the originals.

items.label: Invoices requested
items.detail: Every invoice over £500 for the period

items.label: Supplier contracts
items.detail: Contracts behind two supplier relationships

items.label: Mileage logs
items.detail: The original logs, not a summary

scenes.heading: How the Records Went Missing
scenes.narration: Here's where it went wrong. Originals binned after capture into Dext, contracts lost in a OneDrive reorganisation, and mileage logs sold off with the van.

items.label: Originals thrown away
items.detail: Invoices captured into Dext, then discarded

items.label: Folder deleted
items.detail: Contracts lost when OneDrive was reorganised

items.label: Notebook in the van
items.detail: Mileage logs went when the van was sold

scenes.heading: Three Statutory Regimes
scenes.narration: UK record-keeping has three overlapping statutory regimes, each with different periods and different categories of document.

items.label: HMRC
items.detail: Tax record-keeping rules

items.label: Companies Act 2006
items.detail: Company records requirements

items.label: Limitation Act 1980
items.detail: Periods for bringing legal claims

scenes.heading: How Long Do We Keep This?
scenes.narration: Add the specific rules for VAT, payroll and anti-money laundering, and that question has at least five right answers, depending on what the document is.

items.label: VAT records
items.detail: VAT's 6-year rule

items.label: Payroll records
items.detail: Payroll's 3-year rule

scenes.heading: MTD Needs the Digital Link
scenes.narration: Making Tax Digital doesn't replace the source document. It demands an unbroken digital link from source, to ledger, to return. GDPR's retention principle also applies.

items.label: Source document
items.detail: The original evidence is still needed

items.label: Ledger
items.detail: Digitally linked to the source

items.label: Return
items.detail: Digitally linked to the ledger

scenes.heading: What This Module Covers
scenes.narration: This module is your map: every source document, who originates it, what it posts, how long to keep it, and why Making Tax Digital still needs the source.

scenes.heading: Cash vs Accruals Basis
scenes.subheading: Same invoice, different tax year: why the basis you choose matters
scenes.narration: Welcome to Module 7. The basis a sole trader uses decides which tax year their income lands in, and that can change both the tax computation and the payments on account.

scenes.heading: One invoice, two tax years
scenes.narration: Picture a landscaper who finishes a fourteen thousand pound job in March 2025 and is paid on the 7th of April. On the cash basis it's taxed in 2025 to 26; on the accruals basis, in 2024 to 25.

items.label: Project finished
items.detail: Garden project completed in March 2025

items.label: Invoice raised
items.detail: Income earned and invoiced in March

items.label: Customer pays
items.detail: Cash received in the new tax year

items.label: Taxable year
items.detail: Cash: 2025/26. Accruals: 2024/25

scenes.heading: The rules flipped in April 2024
scenes.narration: From 6 April 2024, cash basis is the default for every unincorporated business, whatever its turnover. The old one hundred and fifty thousand pound threshold has gone, and accruals is now something you elect into.

items.label: Cash basis
items.detail: For all unincorporated businesses, any turnover

items.label: Accruals basis
items.detail: Once standard, now an election out of cash basis

scenes.heading: When cash basis can cost thousands
scenes.narration: For most very small sole traders, cash basis is fine. But for clients with stock, big assets or losses, it can quietly cost thousands, and switching bases can trigger a tax shock no forecast predicted.

items.label: Stock, WIP and debtors
items.detail: Stock, work in progress or large year-end debtors

items.label: Big assets and losses
items.detail: Capital allowances, or losses to set against general income

items.label: Switching bases
items.detail: Transition adjustments can cause an unplanned tax shock

scenes.heading: Who this affects
scenes.narration: These choices apply to unincorporated businesses such as sole traders. Limited companies are unaffected, because the accounting standards FRS 102 and FRS 105 require accruals, full stop.

items.label: Unincorporated businesses
items.detail: Cash basis by default; can elect for accruals

items.label: Limited companies
items.detail: Must use accruals under FRS 102 or FRS 105

scenes.heading: What this module covers
scenes.narration: In this module we'll define both bases properly, cover who can use what after the 2024 reform, work through transition adjustments, and run the which-is-better calculation you should do at every year-end review.

scenes.heading: Dext: Document Capture & Processing
scenes.subheading: The capture layer that sits before your bookkeeping platform
scenes.narration: Dext, formerly Receipt Bank, captures receipts, invoices, bank statements and card slips before they reach the books. It saves hours and leaves a clear audit trail.

scenes.heading: Before and after Dext
scenes.narration: One practice with sixty small business clients spent around two days a week re-typing invoices and stapling receipts. After rolling out Dext, that dropped to two hours, with the same accuracy.

items.label: SME clients
items.detail: A typical practice workload

items.label: Time before Dext
items.detail: Re-typing invoices, stapling receipts

items.label: Time after Dext
items.detail: Same accuracy, better audit trail

scenes.heading: Four upload routes
scenes.narration: Documents reach Dext in four ways: a photo on the mobile app, emailing them in, syncing a drive, or fetching directly from suppliers.

items.label: Mobile photo
items.detail: Snap a receipt on your phone

items.label: Email-in
items.detail: Forward invoices to Dext

items.label: Drive sync
items.detail: Pull files from a synced drive

items.label: Supplier fetch
items.detail: Collect invoices from suppliers

scenes.heading: From document to ledger
scenes.narration: Dext uses optical character recognition and machine learning to read each document, then publishes it to Xero, QuickBooks Online or Sage with the right account code and VAT rate.

items.label: Extract

items.label: Publish
items.detail: To Xero, QBO or Sage with code and VAT rate

scenes.heading: When HMRC asks questions
scenes.narration: Every transaction keeps its source document attached. So if a Schedule 36 notice arrives in 2028, you just click the line in Xero and the original invoice opens.

items.label: Notice arrives
items.detail: A Schedule 36 information notice

items.label: No shoebox hunt
items.detail: Click the line in Xero

items.label: Evidence ready
items.detail: The original invoice opens, MTD digital link

scenes.heading: What this module covers
scenes.narration: We'll cover what Dext is, the four upload routes, supplier rules, multi-VAT splits, publishing, and the dashboard that lets one person manage thirty or more clients.

scenes.heading: Xero: Setup, Reconciliation & Reporting
scenes.subheading: The platform UK SMEs and their accountants run on
scenes.narration: Xero is the default for any practice taking on a new owner-managed company. Its strength is how its parts plug together, so a bookkeeper can close a month in hours, not days.

scenes.heading: Why Xero Matters
scenes.narration: Xero has around 4.4 million subscribers globally and dominates the UK small and medium-sized business segment, so you will meet it constantly in practice.

items.label: Subscribers globally
items.detail: Dominant in the UK SME segment

scenes.heading: The Four Reconciliation Buttons
scenes.narration: On the bank reconciliation screen, every Xero user first learns Match, Create, Transfer and Discuss. These four buttons are the real productivity unlock.

items.label: Match
items.detail: Xero found the invoice or bill: click Yes

items.label: Create
items.detail: New transaction: type the supplier and code

items.label: Transfer
items.detail: Movement between two bank accounts you own

items.label: Discuss
items.detail: Not sure? Flag it, ask the director, come back

scenes.heading: The Discipline Pieces
scenes.narration: Good Xero work also needs discipline: a chart of accounts suited to the client's sector, lock dates protecting closed periods, tracking categories for analysis, and a reusable report pack.

scenes.heading: Tracking Categories vs Bloated COA
scenes.narration: Tracking categories handle analysis such as jobs, departments and branches, so you don't need to bloat the chart of accounts with extra codes.

items.label: Tracking categories
items.detail: Analyse jobs, departments, branches cleanly

items.label: Extra COA codes
items.detail: Bloats the chart of accounts

scenes.heading: What This Module Covers
scenes.narration: In this module we'll cover new organisation setup, bank reconciliation, bills and invoices, lock dates and tracking categories, and the reports that make Xero a management-accounting platform.

scenes.heading: QuickBooks Online: Setup and Workflow
scenes.subheading: Intuit's UK alternative to Xero, and a better fit for many UK SMEs
scenes.narration: Welcome to QuickBooks Online, Intuit's UK product. It roughly matches Xero in features, and it's the better fit for a sizeable minority of UK small and medium-sized businesses.

scenes.heading: Who QBO suits best
scenes.narration: QuickBooks Online tends to suit three kinds of client: businesses with inventory, those with US-facing operations, and owners who already know the desktop QuickBooks of a decade ago.

items.label: US-facing operations

items.label: Desktop QuickBooks users
items.detail: Owners familiar with the version of a decade ago

scenes.narration: There are four plans, Simple Start, Essentials, Plus and Advanced, scaling from one person to 25 users. As a practitioner, you'll use QuickBooks Online Accountant, which is free with multiple client logins.

scenes.narration: Sage Business Cloud Accounting comes in three tiers: Start, Standard and Plus.

scenes.narration: Rather than be everything to everyone, FreeAgent covers the essentials: time and project tracking, invoicing with online payment, expenses with mileage, dividends, and payroll for a handful of staff.

scenes.heading: VAT on Goods After Brexit
scenes.subheading: Domestic sales, exports, imports and the Northern Ireland Protocol
scenes.narration: Post-Brexit, VAT on goods is built around four scenarios, each with its own rules. Getting them right protects your client's cash flow and keeps their VAT return accurate.

scenes.heading: The Four Scenarios
scenes.narration: Here's the map: domestic UK sales, exports from Great Britain, imports into Great Britain, and the special Northern Ireland Protocol rules.

items.label: Domestic UK sales

items.label: Imports into GB

scenes.heading: VAT on Services: Place of Supply
scenes.subheading: Where is the supply made? That decides whose VAT rules apply
scenes.narration: VAT on services lives or dies on one question: where is the place of supply? That country's VAT applies, or its rules may say no VAT at all.

scenes.heading: The General Rule: B2B vs B2C
scenes.narration: For business to business supplies, the place of supply is where the customer belongs. For business to consumer supplies, it's where the supplier belongs.

items.label: Business to business
items.detail: Place of supply is where the customer belongs

items.label: Business to consumer
items.detail: Place of supply is where the supplier belongs

scenes.heading: A UK Marketing Agency
scenes.narration: Picture a UK marketing agency. Invoicing a US business, it doesn't charge UK VAT. Invoicing a US individual, it does. And a UK software company's EU business client reverse-charges the VAT itself.

items.label: Invoice to US business
items.detail: No UK VAT charged

items.label: Invoice to US individual
items.detail: UK VAT is charged

items.label: UK SaaS to EU business
items.detail: The EU business reverse-charges the VAT

scenes.heading: Special Place of Supply Rules
scenes.narration: Some services have special rules. Land services follow the land, events follow the event, restaurant services follow the restaurant, and electronic services to consumers follow the consumer, under the MOSS and OSS rules.

items.label: Land-related services
items.detail: Follow the land

items.label: Events
items.detail: Follow the event

items.label: Restaurant services
items.detail: Follow the restaurant

items.label: Electronic services to B2C
items.detail: Follow the consumer under MOSS and OSS

scenes.heading: The Reverse Charge
scenes.narration: Under the reverse charge, the customer accounts for the VAT instead of the supplier. For services received from abroad, it goes in both Box 1 and Box 4, so the net effect is zero.

items.label: Customer accounts for VAT
items.detail: Instead of the supplier

items.label: Enter in Box 1
items.detail: VAT due on the service received

items.label: Enter in Box 4
items.detail: Reclaimed as input VAT, so net zero

scenes.heading: Getting It Wrong
scenes.narration: Get the place of supply wrong and you either charge VAT you shouldn't, hurting competitiveness and sparking disputes, or fail to charge VAT you should, and face an HMRC assessment later.

items.detail: Lost competitiveness and customer disputes

items.label: Failing to charge VAT

scenes.heading: VAT on Land and Property
scenes.subheading: Why the default is exempt, not standard-rated
scenes.narration: Property VAT is where almost every accountant's first instinct is wrong. The default here is exempt, not standard-rated, so let's get the basics straight.

scenes.heading: The Default Treatments
scenes.narration: New residential builds are zero-rated, existing residential lettings are exempt, and most commercial property transactions are exempt by default too.

items.label: Most commercial property
items.detail: Exempt by default, unless an Option to Tax is made

scenes.heading: The Option to Tax
scenes.narration: An Option to Tax is a binding twenty-year election that locks a commercial property at the standard rate. Owners make it so they can reclaim significant VAT incurred on a build or refurbishment.

items.label: Without the option
items.detail: Input VAT on build or refurb cannot be reclaimed

items.label: With the option
items.detail: Taxable supply, so input VAT can be reclaimed

scenes.heading: Three More Mechanisms
scenes.narration: You also need three more property mechanisms: the Capital Goods Scheme, Transfer of a Going Concern, and relief for DIY housebuilders.

items.label: Capital Goods Scheme
items.detail: Adjustment period for buildings over £250k

items.label: Transfer of Going Concern
items.detail: Property and tenants sold together; strict conditions

items.label: DIY housebuilders' relief
items.detail: A property-specific relief

scenes.heading: Watch Out
scenes.narration: Be careful: the Option to Tax binds you for twenty years, and changing a property's VAT status mid-tenancy is a known trap.

items.label: Option to Tax is binding
items.detail: It locks the property at standard rate

items.label: Status change mid-tenancy
items.detail: Changing VAT status during a tenancy is a trap

scenes.heading: What This Module Covers

scenes.heading: Partial Exemption
scenes.subheading: When a business makes both taxable and exempt supplies, input VAT is restricted
scenes.narration: Welcome to partial exemption. When a business makes both taxable and exempt supplies, it can't simply reclaim all its input VAT, so getting this right really matters.

scenes.heading: Three Types of Input VAT
scenes.narration: Input VAT on costs directly linked to taxable supplies is fully reclaimable, while VAT linked to exempt supplies is not. The tricky part is residual VAT on shared costs like rent, utilities and accountancy fees.

items.label: Taxable supplies
items.detail: Directly attributable: fully reclaimable

items.label: Exempt supplies
items.detail: Directly attributable: not reclaimable

items.label: Residual
items.detail: Shared costs like rent, utilities, accountancy fees

scenes.heading: Handling Residual VAT
scenes.narration: Residual VAT is apportioned using the Standard Method, based on taxable supplies as a percentage of total supplies. Then at year end, the annual adjustment recomputes on annual figures to true up the quarterly approximations.

items.label: Apply Standard Method
items.detail: Taxable supplies as a % of total supplies

items.label: Claim each quarter
items.detail: Quarterly figures are approximations

items.label: Annual adjustment
items.detail: Recompute on annual figures to true up

scenes.heading: The De Minimis Tests
scenes.narration: If exempt input VAT is less than six hundred and twenty-five pounds a month, and also less than half of total input VAT, you can reclaim it all anyway. Both conditions must be met.

items.label: Exempt input VAT per month
items.detail: Must be below this monthly limit

items.label: Share of total input VAT
items.detail: And must also be below half the total

scenes.heading: Getting It Wrong
scenes.narration: Mistakes cost either way. Under-claim and you've handed free money to HMRC; over-claim and you face an HMRC assessment plus a penalty.

items.label: Under-claim
items.detail: Free money handed to HMRC

items.label: Over-claim
items.detail: HMRC assessment plus a penalty

scenes.heading: What This Module Covers
scenes.narration: This is the framework every accountant for landlords, charities, financial services and healthcare providers must run. Here's what we'll cover.

scenes.heading: VAT Errors, Inspections & Penalties
scenes.subheading: Correcting errors, the points system, late payment and HMRC inspections
scenes.narration: Found a VAT error six months after filing? The big question is whether you can fix it on the next return or must disclose it separately. Let's work through the rules and the penalties that follow.

scenes.heading: Correct on return or disclose?
scenes.narration: Net errors up to £10,000, or up to 1% of Box 6 turnover capped at £50,000, can be corrected on your next return. Anything above that needs mandatory disclosure on form VAT652.

items.label: Next return
items.detail: Or up to 1% of Box 6 turnover, capped at £50,000

items.label: Separate disclosure
items.detail: Mandatory for errors above the threshold

scenes.heading: Late filing points thresholds
scenes.narration: Since January 2023, each late filing earns a point. Reach the threshold for your filing frequency and a fixed £200 penalty applies, with another £200 for each later late return until the points expire.

items.label: Quarterly filers
items.detail: Then a fixed £200 penalty

items.label: Monthly filers
items.detail: Then a fixed £200 penalty

items.label: Annual filers
items.detail: Then a fixed £200 penalty

scenes.heading: Late payment penalties
scenes.narration: Late payment penalties are separate. There's 2% at day 16, another 2% at day 31, and then 4% annualised, charged daily.

items.label: First penalty
items.detail: 2% charge

items.label: Second penalty
items.detail: Another 2%

items.label: Ongoing
items.detail: 4% annualised, charged daily

scenes.heading: How a VAT inspection works
scenes.narration: In an inspection, HMRC visits, picks a quarter and tests every box on the return against the underlying records.

items.label: HMRC visits
items.detail: An officer turns up to review your VAT

items.label: A quarter is chosen
items.detail: HMRC selects one return period

items.label: Every box tested
items.detail: Checked against the underlying records

scenes.heading: Behaviour-based penalties
scenes.narration: If tax was underpaid, penalties depend on behaviour: 30% of the underpaid tax for careless, 70% for deliberate, and 100% for deliberate and concealed.

items.label: Careless
items.detail: Of the under-paid tax

items.label: Deliberate
items.detail: Of the under-paid tax

items.label: Deliberate and concealed
items.detail: Of the under-paid tax

scenes.narration: So in this module we'll cover error thresholds, the points-based penalty system, late payment penalties, and how to manage a VAT inspection.

scenes.heading: Making Tax Digital for VAT
scenes.subheading: Digital records plus an unbroken digital link to every box on the return
scenes.narration: Making Tax Digital for VAT has applied to everyone VAT-registered since April 2022. It is really two technical requirements packaged as one regime, and you will need to check both for every client.

scenes.heading: The key facts
scenes.narration: The regime has been live for all VAT-registered businesses since April 2022, and the digital link must run from source records right through to each of the 9 boxes on the return.

items.label: Live for everyone
items.detail: All VAT-registered businesses

items.label: Boxes on the VAT return
items.detail: Each must be fed by an unbroken digital link

scenes.heading: Two requirements, one regime
scenes.narration: First, records must be digital, showing each supply's date, value and VAT rate in functional compatible software. Second, data must move between software by automated transfer, which is the digital link.

items.label: Digital records
items.detail: Date, value and VAT rate in compatible software

items.label: Digital links
items.detail: Automated data transfer between software

items.label: Bridging software
items.detail: Links spreadsheet records to the return

scenes.heading: What keeps the link intact?
scenes.narration: XML, CSV import and export, and API calls all preserve the digital link. Re-typing a number across systems breaks it, and technically so does cut and paste.

items.label: Preserves the link
items.detail: XML, CSV import or export, API calls

items.label: Breaks the link
items.detail: Re-typing figures, or cut and paste

scenes.heading: Penalties add up
scenes.narration: The compliance penalty isn't huge for each incident, but it can be assessed alongside any other VAT penalty, so it soon adds up. And remember, the soft-landing periods are now closed.

items.detail: Modest alone, but can sit alongside other VAT penalties

items.label: Soft-landing periods
items.detail: No more grace for broken links

scenes.heading: PAYE Fundamentals
scenes.subheading: Tax codes, NI categories and Real Time Information for UK payroll
scenes.narration: When you run payroll for a UK employer, you're acting as HMRC's unpaid tax collector. Every error comes back to you within about four weeks, so getting the fundamentals right really matters.

scenes.heading: The payroll duties
scenes.narration: You collect Income Tax through PAYE and employee National Insurance, pay employer National Insurance on top, file the Full Payment Submission when pay reaches the employee's bank, and pay HMRC by the 22nd.

items.label: Collect tax and NI
items.detail: Income Tax via PAYE plus employee NI

items.label: Pay employer NI
items.detail: Paid on top of employee deductions

items.label: File the FPS
items.detail: When payment hits the employee's bank

items.label: Pay HMRC
items.detail: By the 22nd

scenes.heading: Tax codes: HMRC's language
scenes.narration: Tax codes are how HMRC tells you how much to deduct. You'll meet 1257L, BR, NT and K codes, S and C prefixes for Scottish and Welsh taxpayers, and week 1 month 1 emergency codes.

items.label: Others
items.detail: Veterans, freeport, deferred

scenes.narration: The Full Payment Submission goes on or before each payment, while the Employer Payment Summary covers adjustments and CIS recovery. Newly qualified bookkeepers often mix these up.

items.label: EPS
items.detail: Employer Payment Summary, adjustments and CIS recovery

scenes.heading: Statutory Payments
scenes.subheading: Sick pay, parental pay and bereavement pay: what employers pay and reclaim
scenes.narration: When an employee goes off sick, becomes a parent or loses a baby, the employer must pay statutory amounts. Most of them can be reclaimed, so getting them right really matters.

scenes.heading: The six statutory payments
scenes.narration: There are six: statutory sick pay, maternity, paternity, shared parental, adoption and parental bereavement pay. Sick pay is the odd one out, because it is not reclaimable.

items.label: Statutory Sick Pay

items.detail: Statutory maternity and paternity pay

items.label: Parental Bereavement
items.detail: Statutory parental bereavement pay

scenes.narration: Small employers, with Class 1 National Insurance of forty-five thousand pounds or less in the previous year, recover 103 percent; the extra 3 percent covers employer National Insurance. Standard employers reclaim 92 percent.

items.detail: Class 1 NI of £45k or less in the previous year

items.label: Standard employers
items.detail: Of statutory pay paid

items.label: Statutory Sick Pay

scenes.narration: Mistakes cost either way. Underpay, and the employee gets less than they are entitled to, leading to an HR claim. Overpay, and you cannot reclaim the excess from HMRC.

scenes.narration: As an accountant, you must apply each eligibility test: qualifying days for sick pay, the qualifying week for maternity pay, the 26-week service requirement, and the paternity, shared parental and adoption windows.

scenes.heading: Auto-Enrolment Pensions
scenes.subheading: Workplace pensions are mandatory for every UK employer with at least one worker
scenes.narration: Since the Pensions Act 2008, every UK employer with at least one worker must provide a workplace pension. Let's look at what that means in practice for the employers you'll advise.

scenes.narration: On each pay date, every employee is put into one of three categories. Only the eligible ones must be automatically enrolled into a qualifying scheme.

items.label: Eligible

items.label: Non-eligible
items.detail: Not automatically enrolled

items.label: Entitled
items.detail: Not automatically enrolled

items.label: Employer contribution
items.detail: Minimum, on qualifying earnings

items.label: Employee contribution
items.detail: Minimum deduction from qualifying earnings

scenes.heading: Benefits in Kind and P11D Reporting
scenes.subheading: Non-cash perks from employment: how they're taxed, valued and reported
scenes.narration: A benefit in kind is any non-cash advantage an employer provides by reason of employment, like a company car, private medical cover or a phone used personally. Getting them right matters for both employee and employer.

scenes.heading: Who Pays What
scenes.narration: Benefits in kind are taxable on the employee under the Income Tax Earnings and Pensions Act 2003. The employer pays Class 1A National Insurance: 13.8% for 2024 to 25, rising to 15% in 2025 to 26.

items.detail: Charged on the employer

items.label: Class 1A NI 2025/26
items.detail: The employer rate rises

scenes.narration: Each common benefit has its own valuation rule. A company car uses list price times a carbon dioxide based percentage, private medical uses cost to the employer, and private fuel uses the fuel multiplier times that percentage.

items.label: Private medical
items.detail: Cost to the employer

items.label: Private fuel

scenes.heading: Construction Industry Scheme

scenes.narration: The Construction Industry Scheme, or CIS, is how HMRC taxes payments to subcontractors at source. It was designed in the 1970s to combat the cash economy in construction, and it's still essential today.

scenes.subheading: Turning the running ledger into true and fair statutory accounts

scenes.subheading: Small company accounts: the most-used disclosure regime in UK practice
scenes.narration: Section 1A sits between the austerity of FRS 105 and the heavy disclosure burden of full FRS 102. It's the bread-and-butter framework of UK small and medium-sized business accounting, so you'll use it constantly.

scenes.heading: Who counts as small?
scenes.narration: A small company has turnover up to £10.2 million, assets up to £5.1 million and no more than 50 employees. From 6 April 2025 the first two rise to £15 million and £7.5 million, while employees stay at 50.

scenes.heading: Corporation Tax Fundamentals
scenes.subheading: The tax on UK company profits, and the framework behind every CT600
scenes.narration: Corporation Tax is the levy on UK company profits. This module is the scaffold for everything in Part 6, giving you the language, the deadlines and the rate map you'll use on every return.

scenes.heading: Two Acts govern Corporation Tax
scenes.narration: Two Acts set the rules. The Corporation Tax Act 2009 deals with income and expenses, while the Corporation Tax Act 2010 covers rates, reliefs and groups.

scenes.narration: Since 1 April 2023 there are two rates: nineteen percent on profits up to fifty thousand pounds, and twenty-five percent from two hundred and fifty thousand. Marginal relief tapers between, at an effective marginal rate of about 26.5 percent.

scenes.heading: Loss & Group Relief

scenes.heading: Five trading-loss reliefs
scenes.narration: The Corporation Tax Act 2010, from section 37 onward, gives five separate trading-loss reliefs. Each one uses the loss at a different time or in a different company.

items.label: Current year

scenes.heading: How far back and forward
scenes.narration: Ordinary carry back reaches 12 months, while terminal loss relief on cessation under section 39 reaches back three years. Since 1 April 2017, carried-forward losses can relieve total profits, not just trading profits.

items.label: Terminal loss relief

items.label: Full relief allowance
items.detail: Profits that brought-forward losses can fully relieve

items.label: Above the allowance
items.detail: Only half of profits over £5m can be relieved

scenes.heading: Group and consortium relief
scenes.narration: Group relief, under Part 5 of the Act, lets a company surrender losses to a group or consortium member. It runs on a strict ownership test, and both companies must be UK-resident or chargeable to corporation tax.

items.label: 75% group
items.detail: Strict ownership test applies

items.label: 75% consortium
items.detail: Surrender to a consortium member

items.label: Residence condition
items.detail: Both UK-resident or chargeable to CT

scenes.heading: What this module covers
scenes.narration: Different losses, like loan relationship deficits, property losses and management expenses, each have their own rules. We'll map every relief, every restriction, and the order to claim them in.

scenes.heading: CT600 Walkthrough in TaxCalc
scenes.subheading: Completing and filing the Corporation Tax Return in software
scenes.narration: The CT600 is the Corporation Tax Return, covering every type of UK company income, deduction and payment. In this module we walk through filing one end to end in TaxCalc.

scenes.heading: The CT600 at a glance
scenes.narration: It's a big form, with twelve sections and around a hundred boxes. That's why, in practice, Corporation Tax returns are submitted through tax software.

items.label: Sections
items.detail: Covering income, deductions and payments

items.label: Boxes
items.detail: Every type of UK company income

scenes.heading: Tax software options
scenes.narration: Practices use packages such as TaxCalc, IRIS, CCH and Sage. We'll use TaxCalc, as it's the most accessible example of the workflow.

items.label: TaxCalc
items.detail: Used in this module as the accessible example

scenes.heading: Key box ranges
scenes.narration: The boxes run in order, from company information and profits, through losses and the tax calculation, to capital allowances, reliefs claimed and finally tax payable.

items.label: Turnover and profits
items.detail: Property and investment income at 155-205

items.label: Losses and tax calc
items.detail: Losses brought forward, then calculation and reliefs

items.label: Capital allowances
items.detail: R&D and creative reliefs at 475-515

items.label: Tax payable
items.detail: After deductions and reliefs claimed at 695-779

scenes.heading: What attaches to the CT600
scenes.narration: Every return attaches the iXBRL accounts and computation. Supplementary pages are added only where relevant, such as close-company loans, groups, losses or tax avoidance disclosure.

items.label: iXBRL files
items.detail: Accounts and tax computation

items.label: CT600A and CT600B
items.detail: Close-company loans; group

items.label: CT600C and CT600J
items.detail: Losses; disclosure of tax avoidance

scenes.heading: What this module covers
scenes.narration: We'll set up and import data from accounts production, complete a typical small company return, validate it, submit it through the HMRC gateway, and look at the receipt.

scenes.heading: SA100: The Main Tax Return
scenes.subheading: The headline personal return every UK Self Assessment client files each year
scenes.narration: The SA100 is the headline personal tax return that every UK Self Assessment client files each year. It captures income from all sources, applies deductions and allowances, and works out the tax due.

scenes.heading: Supplementary Pages
scenes.narration: The main return is supplemented by source-specific pages, such as SA102 for employment, SA103 for self-employment, SA105 for UK property and SA108 for capital gains. Others cover partnerships, foreign income and residence.

items.label: SA102 Employment
items.detail: Income from a job

items.label: SA103 Self-employment
items.detail: Sole trader profits

items.label: SA105 UK property
items.detail: Rental income from UK property

items.label: SA108 Capital gains
items.detail: Also SA104, SA106 and SA109 pages

scenes.heading: Who Files and How
scenes.narration: Under section 8 of the Taxes Management Act 1970, anyone who receives a notice to file must file. Most returns go online through the HMRC Personal Tax Account or commercial software, though paper is still accepted for some categories.

items.label: Online
items.detail: Personal Tax Account, TaxCalc, Sage, BTCSoftware, Andica

items.label: Paper
items.detail: Still accepted for some categories

scenes.heading: Key Dates
scenes.narration: Paper returns are due by 31 October and online returns by 31 January. The balancing payment and first payment on account are also due 31 January, with the second payment on account due 31 July.

items.label: Online return and payments
items.detail: Balancing payment and first payment on account

scenes.heading: Late Filing Penalties
scenes.narration: Penalties escalate fast. There's an immediate £100, then £10 a day after three months up to £900, then 5% or £300 at six and again at twelve months.

items.label: Immediate penalty
items.detail: As soon as the return is late

items.label: Daily after 3 months
items.detail: Up to a maximum of £900

items.label: At 6 and 12 months
items.detail: Charged at each point

scenes.heading: What This Module Covers
scenes.narration: In this module we'll walk through the return's structure, who must register and when, how income and allowances flow, and the full software workflow from start to finish.

scenes.heading: SA103: Reporting Self-Employment
scenes.subheading: How sole traders report self-employed income on the SA100 tax return
scenes.narration: The SA103 is the part of the SA100 tax return where self-employed income is reported. Getting it right matters, because recent reforms have changed how sole traders are taxed.

scenes.heading: Two Versions of the SA103
scenes.narration: There are two versions. The short form suits turnover up to around eighty-five thousand pounds, while the full form is for higher turnover or more complex claims such as Construction Industry Scheme deductions.

items.label: SA103S Short
items.detail: For simpler cases with turnover up to the threshold

items.label: SA103F Full
items.detail: Also for CIS deductions, car allowances, unusual reliefs

scenes.heading: Basis Period Reform
scenes.narration: From 2024 to 25, sole traders report profits on a tax-year basis, replacing the old current year basis. Traders whose accounts don't end on 31 March need transition profit calculations, spread over five years.

items.label: Tax-year basis applies
items.detail: Fully effective, replacing the current year basis

items.label: Tax year runs
items.detail: Profits now reported for this period

items.label: Transition profits spread
items.detail: For non-31-March accounting periods, under FA 2022

scenes.heading: National Insurance Changes
scenes.narration: Class 4 National Insurance on profits between twelve thousand five hundred and seventy and fifty thousand two hundred and seventy pounds fell to eight percent from 6 April 2024. Class 2 was abolished for profits above the small profits threshold.

items.label: Class 4 main rate
items.detail: From 6 April 2024, down from 9%

items.label: Class 4 profit band
items.detail: Lower limit; band runs up to £50,270

items.label: Class 2 NIC
items.detail: From April 2024, above the small profits threshold

scenes.heading: Key Reliefs and Methods
scenes.narration: Under the Finance Act 2023, the cash basis is now the default for sole traders and partners. And the one thousand pound trading allowance can shelter small side incomes.

items.label: Cash basis default
items.detail: Now the default for sole traders and partners

items.label: Trading allowance
items.detail: Shelters small side incomes

scenes.heading: What This Module Covers
scenes.narration: In this module we'll walk through the SA103, the basis period reform, National Insurance changes, choosing cash or accruals, the annual investment allowance, and handling CIS deductions for subcontractors.

scenes.heading: SA105: Property Income
scenes.subheading: How individuals report UK property income on their tax return
scenes.narration: The SA105 is where individuals report UK property income, from buy-to-let landlords to rent-a-room hosts. Getting it right matters, because a few big rules shape how much tax landlords pay.

scenes.heading: Section 24: mortgage interest
scenes.narration: Under Section 24, from Finance Act 2016, mortgage interest is no longer deducted since 2020 to 2021. Instead there's a 20% basic-rate tax credit, which hits higher-rate residential landlords hard, as they now pay tax on gross rents.

items.label: Before
items.detail: Mortgage interest deducted from rental income

items.label: Since 2020/21
items.detail: Basic-rate tax credit replaces the deduction

scenes.heading: Two key tax-free amounts
scenes.narration: The property allowance lets £1,000 of letting income go tax-free, but you either take it or deduct actual expenses, never both. Rent-a-Room shelters up to £7,500 a year for a furnished room in your main home.

items.label: Property allowance
items.detail: Tax-free, or deduct actual expenses, not both

items.label: Rent-a-Room scheme
items.detail: Per year, furnished room in your main home

scenes.heading: Furnished holiday lets abolished
scenes.narration: From 6 April 2025 the furnished holiday lettings regime is abolished. Former holiday lets become standard residential lets, with all the Section 24 disadvantages and the loss of several valuable reliefs.

items.label: No full mortgage interest
items.detail: Section 24 restriction now applies

items.label: No capital allowances
items.detail: Lost for ex-FHL properties

items.label: No BADR on disposal
items.detail: Business Asset Disposal Relief no longer available

scenes.heading: Who is affected?
scenes.narration: These changes bite hardest on individual residential landlords. Commercial property and corporate landlords are largely unaffected, which is why many landlords eventually ask whether to incorporate.

items.label: Residential landlords
items.detail: Hit by Section 24 and FHL abolition

items.label: Commercial and corporate
items.detail: Largely unaffected

scenes.heading: What this module covers
scenes.narration: In this module we'll work through Section 24 with a worked example, the property allowance, Rent-a-Room, the post-2025 holiday let position, and the big question: incorporate or stay personal?

scenes.heading: SA108: Capital Gains
scenes.subheading: Reporting gains and losses for individuals under TCGA 1992
scenes.narration: Welcome to Module 44. The SA108 is where individuals report their capital gains and losses, under the Taxation of Chargeable Gains Act 1992, and the rules have shifted a lot recently.

scenes.heading: Annual Exempt Amount slashed
scenes.narration: The Annual Exempt Amount has been cut sharply, from twelve thousand three hundred pounds in 2022 to 23, down to just three thousand pounds for 2024 to 25.

scenes.heading: Two sets of CGT rates
scenes.narration: Most assets are taxed at 10 or 20 percent, depending on whether you're a basic or higher rate taxpayer. Residential property is 18 or 24 percent, with the higher rate cut from 28 percent in April 2024.

items.label: Most assets
items.detail: Basic rate / higher rate

items.label: Residential property
items.detail: Higher rate cut from 28% in April 2024

scenes.heading: Business Asset Disposal Relief
scenes.narration: Business Asset Disposal Relief gives a lower rate on qualifying business sales, up to a one million pound lifetime allowance. But that rate is rising: 10 percent now, 14 percent from April 2025, and 18 percent from April 2026.

items.label: Current rate
items.detail: Up to £1m lifetime allowance

scenes.heading: Share matching order
scenes.narration: Under section 106A, shares sold are matched in a strict order: first same-day purchases, then those bought in the next 30 days, and finally the section 104 pool.

items.label: Same day
items.detail: Match shares bought on the day of sale

items.label: Next 30 days
items.detail: Then shares bought within 30 days

items.label: Section 104 pool
items.detail: Then the pooled holding

scenes.heading: The 60-day trap for landlords
scenes.narration: Residential property gains need a separate capital gains tax return online with HMRC within 60 days, as well as reporting on the SA108 at year-end. This catches landlords out every year.

items.label: Separate CGT return
items.detail: Via HMRC Online, not on the SA108

scenes.heading: What this module covers
scenes.narration: We'll walk through all the rates and the exempt amount, relief for business sales, share pooling, main home and letting relief, and that crucial 60-day reporting rule.

scenes.heading: SA104: Partnership Income
scenes.subheading: How partners are taxed on their share of partnership profit
scenes.narration: Partnerships are transparent for tax. The partnership itself doesn't pay tax; instead, each partner's share of profit is taxed on their own personal return.

scenes.heading: Two Filings Required
scenes.narration: Two filings are needed. A nominated partner submits the SA800 partnership return with the profit allocation, and each partner adds the SA104 supplementary pages to their own SA100.

items.label: SA800 partnership return
items.detail: Nominated partner submits the profit allocation

items.label: SA104 supplementary
items.detail: Each partner files it with their SA100

scenes.heading: Who Can Be a Partner
scenes.narration: Partners can be individuals, who report on the SA104, or companies, who report their share on the CT600. Corporate partners bring special rules and anti-avoidance provisions.

items.label: Individual partners
items.detail: Share reported on the SA104

items.label: Corporate partners
items.detail: Share reported on the CT600

scenes.heading: LLP Salaried Members Rule
scenes.narration: For LLPs, the salaried members rule in section 863A of the Income Tax Act 2007 is critical. Meet all three tests and the member is deemed an employee for PAYE and National Insurance, an expensive surprise.

items.label: Disguised salary
items.detail: More than 80% of the member's pay-out

items.label: No significant influence
items.detail: Member lacks significant influence over the LLP

items.label: Low capital contribution
items.detail: Contribution under 25% of the pay-out

scenes.heading: Basis-Period Reform for Partners
scenes.narration: Basis-period reform applies to partners too. From 2024 to 25, profits are taxed on a tax-year basis, with transition profit spread and overlap profits used up.

items.label: Tax-year basis
items.detail: Profits taxed on a tax-year basis from this year

items.label: Transition profit
items.detail: Transition profit is spread

items.label: Overlap profits
items.detail: Overlap profits are used up

scenes.heading: What This Module Covers
scenes.narration: In this module we'll walk through the SA104, SA800 mechanics, the LLP salaried members test, the mixed membership rules that catch profit-shifting, and the partner versus employee distinction HMRC scrutinises closely.

scenes.heading: SA109: Residence and Domicile
scenes.subheading: Deciding whether the UK taxes worldwide income or only UK source income
scenes.narration: Welcome to the SA109, the form that reports residence and domicile status. It's the gatekeeper that decides whether the UK taxes someone on their worldwide income or only on their UK source income.

scenes.heading: The Statutory Residence Test
scenes.narration: The Statutory Residence Test, set out in Schedule 45 of the Finance Act 2013, works as a three-tier flow. You check the automatic overseas tests first, then the automatic UK tests, then the sufficient ties test.

items.label: Automatic overseas tests
items.detail: Checked first: is the person automatically non-resident?

items.label: Automatic UK tests
items.detail: Next: is the person automatically UK resident?

items.label: Sufficient ties test
items.detail: Family, accommodation, 90-day, work and country ties

scenes.heading: Automatic Overseas vs Automatic UK
scenes.narration: You're automatically overseas with under 16 days in the UK, or under 46 if non-resident in the three prior years, or with full-time work abroad. You're automatically UK resident with 183 days or more, your only home here, or full-time UK work.

items.label: Automatic overseas
items.detail: Or under 46 days if non-resident 3 prior years; or full-time overseas work

items.label: Automatic UK
items.detail: Or only home in the UK; or full-time UK work

scenes.heading: Arrivals, Departures and Big Changes
scenes.narration: In years when someone arrives or leaves, split-year treatment can apply, with eight cases to know. And the big news: from 6 April 2025, the two-hundred-year-old non-dom remittance basis was abolished.

items.label: Split-year treatment
items.detail: Applies in years of arrival or departure

items.label: Remittance basis abolished
items.detail: Ends a regime around 200 years old

items.label: New FIG regime
items.detail: For new arrivals, plus transition rules

scenes.heading: How the Non-Dom Shelter Closed
scenes.narration: Deemed domicile rules, based on 15 or 20 years of UK residence, already brought many non-doms into inheritance tax. The Foreign Income and Gains regime now ends the income tax shelter too.

items.label: Deemed domicile
items.detail: UK residence brought many non-doms into inheritance tax

items.label: FIG regime
items.detail: Foreign Income and Gains rules end the income tax shelter

scenes.heading: What This Module Covers
scenes.narration: In this module we'll walk through the residence test with worked examples, split-year treatment, the FIG regime and its transition rules, and the SA109 boxes that report it all.

scenes.heading: Tax Calculation & Payments on Account
scenes.subheading: How UK personal tax is built: income types, allowances and stacked bands
scenes.narration: UK personal tax isn't a flat charge. It comes from sorting income by type, tapering allowances and stacking bands in a set order, so getting the order right is everything.

scenes.heading: 2024/25 Rates and Bands
scenes.narration: Here are the 2024 to 25 figures. The Personal Allowance is £12,570, basic rate is 20% up to £50,270, higher rate 40% up to £125,140, and additional rate 45% above that.

items.label: Personal Allowance
items.detail: Lost £1 per £2 over £100k; gone at £125,140

scenes.heading: The Order Income Is Taxed
scenes.narration: Order matters. Earned and property income go first, then savings, then dividends, and each fills its bands in turn, which decides the rate every pound pays.

items.label: Earned and property income
items.detail: Fills the bands first

items.label: Savings income
items.detail: £5k 0% starting rate; PSA £1,000 BR or £500 HR

scenes.heading: Payments on Account
scenes.narration: Payments on account are each 50% of last year's liability, due on 31 January and 31 July. They're waived if under £1,000 is due or over 80% was taxed at source.

items.label: First payment on account
items.detail: 50% of prior-year liability

items.label: Second payment on account
items.detail: 50% of prior-year liability

scenes.heading: National Insurance Changes
scenes.narration: For the self-employed, Class 2 National Insurance was abolished for 2024 to 25, while Class 4 still applies to profits at 8% and 2%.

items.label: Class 4
items.detail: On self-employed profits

scenes.heading: What This Module Covers
scenes.narration: We'll walk the calculation step by step, with worked examples for typical clients, from employees with side income to landlords and business owners.

scenes.heading: Self Assessment Reliefs
scenes.subheading: Pension, Gift Aid, EIS, SEIS and VCT: the levers of personal tax planning
scenes.narration: Personal tax planning lives in the Self Assessment reliefs. They extend tax bands, reduce the tax due and shelter capital, so knowing them well really pays off for your clients.

scenes.heading: Pension Contributions
scenes.narration: Pension contributions get tax relief at the marginal rate. The annual allowance rose to sixty thousand pounds from 2023 to 24, but it tapers for high earners, down to ten thousand pounds.

items.label: Annual allowance
items.detail: From 2023/24, previously £40k

items.label: Threshold income test
items.detail: Taper applies above this

items.label: Adjusted income test
items.detail: Also needed for taper to apply

items.label: Minimum tapered allowance
items.detail: Lowest the allowance can fall to

scenes.heading: Lifetime Allowance Replaced
scenes.narration: The lifetime allowance was abolished from 6 April 2024. In its place come two new limits: the lump sum allowance, and the lump sum and death benefit allowance.

items.label: Lump-sum allowance
items.detail: Replaces part of the old lifetime allowance

items.label: Lump-sum and death benefit
items.detail: Wider allowance including death benefits

scenes.heading: Investment Reliefs
scenes.narration: For investors, there are three schemes. The Seed Enterprise Investment Scheme, the Enterprise Investment Scheme and Venture Capital Trusts each give income tax relief, with different rates and limits.

items.label: SEIS
items.detail: On up to £200k; CGT exempt after 3 years

items.label: EIS
items.detail: On up to £1m, or £2m if knowledge-intensive

items.label: VCT
items.detail: On up to £200k; tax-free dividends, CGT exempt

scenes.heading: Gift Aid and Other Reliefs
scenes.narration: Gift Aid extends a donor's basic rate band by one and a quarter times the gift, because the charity reclaims twenty percent. Don't forget Marriage Allowance and blind person's allowance either.

items.label: A client gives to charity
items.detail: The donation is made under Gift Aid

items.label: Charity reclaims tax
items.detail: This grosses the gift up

items.label: Basic rate band extends
items.detail: Band grows by 1.25 times the gift

items.label: Marriage Allowance
items.detail: Transfer available, plus blind person's allowance

scenes.heading: What This Module Covers
scenes.narration: In this module we'll work through each relief mechanism, the boxes on the SA100 return and supplementary pages, and the order to claim reliefs to get the most benefit.

scenes.heading: Choosing a Business Structure
scenes.subheading: The decision framework for UK business advisory
scenes.narration: Structure choice is the highest-leverage decision in UK business advisory. It sets tax exposure, liability protection, privacy, capital flexibility and compliance burden for years.

scenes.heading: The Five Canonical Options
scenes.narration: There are five standard options, from the simple sole trader with full personal liability, through partnerships and limited liability partnerships, to private limited companies and public limited companies.

items.label: Sole trader
items.detail: Zero set-up, full liability, Self Assessment only

items.label: Partnership
items.detail: Joint and several liability, SA800 plus SA104s

items.label: LLP
items.detail: Limited liability, tax transparent, public accounts

items.label: Private Ltd and PLC
items.detail: Limited liability, Corporation Tax; PLC is listed-ready

scenes.heading: Five Questions Drive the Decision
scenes.narration: The decision turns on five questions: how much liability the client will accept, their profit profile, privacy concerns, capital plans, and how complex the operation is.

items.label: Liability appetite
items.detail: How much personal risk is acceptable?

items.label: Profit profile
items.detail: Low, lumpy or growing?

items.label: Privacy concerns
items.detail: Are public accounts a problem?

items.label: Capital plans
items.detail: Will the business need shares?

items.label: Operational complexity
items.detail: How complex is the business to run?

scenes.heading: Tax-Driver Rules of Thumb
scenes.narration: Under thirty thousand pounds profit, sole trader typically wins, with no double tax and no public accounts. Thirty to fifty thousand is a grey zone, and above fifty thousand a limited company usually wins.

items.label: Sole trader typically wins
items.detail: No double tax, no public accounts

items.label: Grey zone
items.detail: Depends on how profits are extracted

items.label: Ltd usually wins
items.detail: Salary and dividend optimisation

items.label: Ltd essential
items.detail: Capital allowances and growth investors

scenes.heading: The Common Advisor Mistake
scenes.narration: Many advisors choose poorly because they default to a limited company without modelling the options. Always test the client's figures against the framework first.

items.label: Defaulting to Ltd
items.detail: Choosing without modelling leads to poor outcomes

scenes.heading: What This Module Covers
scenes.narration: In this module you'll get the decision framework, a worked example, and a cheat-sheet to use in first meetings with clients.

scenes.heading: Sole Trader Setup
scenes.subheading: Simple to start, but tax compliance still needs precision
scenes.narration: Setting up as a sole trader is deceptively simple: no Companies House registration, no Articles, no shareholders and no minutes. But the tax compliance still requires real precision.

scenes.heading: The Legal Status
scenes.narration: Here's the key point: the trader is the business. There's no separate legal person, so the trader has full personal liability for the business's debts and to its creditors.

items.label: No separate legal person
items.detail: The trader and the business are one and the same

items.label: Full personal liability
items.detail: Personal liability for all debts and creditors

scenes.heading: Getting Registered
scenes.narration: First, register for Self Assessment using form CWF1. HM Revenue and Customs issues a Unique Taxpayer Reference in about ten days, then you activate Government Gateway and ideally open a separate business bank account.

items.label: Register via CWF1
items.detail: Self Assessment registration, with Class 4 NIC

items.label: Receive your UTR
items.detail: HMRC issues it in around 10 days

items.label: Activate Government Gateway
items.detail: Your online access to HMRC

items.label: Business bank account
items.detail: Strongly recommended, not legally required

scenes.heading: Don't Miss the CWF1 Deadline
scenes.narration: Register by the fifth of October after the tax year you started trading. Miss it and you could face a failure-to-notify penalty of up to one hundred percent of the tax due.

items.label: Failure-to-notify penalty
items.detail: Of tax due, if not registered by 5 October

scenes.heading: Further Setup Decisions
scenes.narration: Next, register for VAT if turnover exceeds the ninety thousand pound threshold for 2024 to 25, and for PAYE if you hire. Cash basis is now the default, and new traders report on a tax-year basis from day one.

items.label: VAT registration
items.detail: Turnover threshold for 2024/25

items.label: PAYE registration
items.detail: Needed if hiring employees

items.label: Cash or accruals
items.detail: Cash basis is default from 24/25; accruals by election

items.label: Basis period reform
items.detail: New traders report on a tax-year basis from day one

scenes.heading: What This Module Covers
scenes.narration: Sole traders are cheap to set up and run, but pay full income tax and Class 4 National Insurance on profits. In this module, we'll cover each step, the mechanics, the delayed Making Tax Digital timeline and a year-one checklist.

scenes.heading: Setting Up a Partnership
scenes.subheading: Why careful setup matters when every partner is personally exposed
scenes.narration: A general partnership exists the moment two or more persons carry on a business in common with a view of profit. No Companies House registration is needed, but setup needs real care.

scenes.heading: Joint and Several Liability
scenes.narration: Here's why care matters. Joint and several liability exposes every partner personally to the debts and acts of every other partner.

items.label: Personal exposure
items.detail: Each partner is liable for the others' debts and acts

scenes.heading: Agreement vs 1890 Defaults
scenes.narration: A Partnership Agreement overrides the default rules of the Partnership Act 1890. Without one, the defaults govern, and often badly.

items.label: With an agreement
items.detail: Partners set their own terms, overriding the defaults

items.label: No agreement
items.detail: Equal profit shares, equal capital, no salaries

scenes.heading: Six Setup Steps
scenes.narration: First draft the agreement, then register the partnership with HMRC on form SA400 and each partner for Self Assessment on SA401. Nominate a partner for the SA800, open a joint bank account, then add other registrations.

items.label: Draft the agreement
items.detail: Profit share, capital, drawings, exits, disputes

items.label: Register via SA400
items.detail: HMRC issues the partnership tax reference

items.label: Partners file SA401
items.detail: Each partner registers for Self Assessment

items.label: Nominate SA800 partner
items.detail: One partner handles the partnership return

items.label: Bank, VAT and PAYE
items.detail: All partners on the mandate; register as needed

scenes.heading: The LLP Route
scenes.narration: Limited liability partnerships follow a parallel but more formal process. You register with Companies House on form LL IN01, a binding member agreement applies, and accounts must be filed.

items.label: Form LL IN01
items.detail: Registration with Companies House

items.label: Member agreement
items.detail: Binding agreement between members

items.label: Account filing
items.detail: Filing obligations apply

scenes.heading: What This Module Covers
scenes.narration: In this module we'll cover both the general partnership and LLP routes, revisit the salaried members trap from Module 45, and work through the year one checklist.

scenes.heading: Setting Up a Limited Company
scenes.subheading: Companies Act 2006: the advisory task that starts 30+ years of compliance
scenes.narration: Setting up a limited company under the Companies Act 2006 is bread-and-butter advisory work. It matters because this one decision exposes your client to more than thirty years of compliance obligations.

scenes.heading: Pre-Incorporation Decisions
scenes.narration: Before incorporating, agree the key details. Check the name is available on WebCheck, use your office as a service address for privacy, and remember directors must be sixteen or over and not disqualified.

items.label: Company name
items.detail: Check WebCheck; no Crown or charity implication

items.label: Addresses
items.detail: Registered office is public; use accountant for service

items.label: Directors and PSCs
items.detail: Directors not disqualified; record significant control

items.label: Shares and SIC codes
items.detail: Typically 100 £1 ordinary shares; 1 to 4 SIC codes

scenes.heading: Incorporation via Form IN01
scenes.narration: You incorporate online using form IN01. The standard fee is fifty pounds, or seventy-eight pounds for same-day, and the company registration number usually arrives within hours.

items.label: Standard filing fee
items.detail: Online IN01 application

items.label: Same-day filing fee
items.detail: For urgent incorporations

items.label: Registration number
items.detail: Company registration number issued quickly

scenes.heading: Post-Incorporation: Week One
scenes.narration: In the first week, get the certificate, open a bank account, and confirm Corporation Tax registration to get the tax reference. Expect the bank to be slower because of ownership checks.

items.label: Certificate
items.detail: Certificate of incorporation received

items.label: Bank account
items.detail: PSC and beneficial owner checks slow this

items.label: HMRC registration
items.detail: Corporation Tax auto-triggered; get the UTR

items.label: Statutory records
items.detail: Shareholder, director and PSC registers, books

scenes.heading: ECCTA 2024 Changes
scenes.narration: The Economic Crime and Corporate Transparency Act 2024 brings big changes. From autumn 2025 all directors and people with significant control must verify identity, and filing becomes software-only from 2027.

items.label: Identity verification
items.detail: Unverified directors cannot file or act

items.label: Software-only filing
items.detail: Filing moves to software only

scenes.heading: What This Module Covers
scenes.narration: We'll walk through every step of setup, the practical pitfalls such as PSC inheritance, share classes and articles, and finish with the first-year compliance calendar.

scenes.heading: Setting Up an LLP
scenes.subheading: A legal person like a company, taxed like a partnership
scenes.narration: A Limited Liability Partnership is the hybrid form, created by the Limited Liability Partnerships Act 2000. It gives members limited liability with partner-style flexibility over profits.

scenes.heading: The Hybrid: Company Meets Partnership
scenes.narration: Like a company, an LLP can sue, own assets and enter contracts. But for tax it's transparent like a partnership, so each member is taxed on their share.

items.label: Like a company
items.detail: Legal person: sues, owns assets, contracts

items.label: Like a partnership
items.detail: Tax-transparent: members taxed on their share

scenes.heading: Five Setup Steps
scenes.narration: Draft the member agreement first, because the Act's defaults mean equal profit shares and everyone consenting to every decision. Then file LL IN01, appoint designated members, register with HMRC, and open a bank account.

items.label: Member Agreement
items.detail: Without one: equal profits, all consent to all decisions

items.label: File LL IN01
items.detail: At Companies House, about 24 hours

items.label: Designated members
items.detail: At least 2: sign accounts, appoint auditors, file CS01

items.label: Register with HMRC
items.detail: SA400 for the LLP, SA401 for each member

scenes.heading: Key Setup Figures
scenes.narration: Incorporating costs fifty pounds and takes around twenty-four hours, and you'll need at least two designated members carrying statutory duties.

items.label: LL IN01 filing fee
items.detail: Paid to Companies House

items.label: Typical turnaround
items.detail: For incorporation

items.label: Designated members
items.detail: Minimum, with statutory duties

scenes.heading: Critical Traps
scenes.narration: Watch out: annual accounts are public at Companies House, ECCTA 2024 identity checks apply to all members, and the salaried members rule can reclassify members as employees.

items.label: Public accounts
items.detail: Annual accounts are public at Companies House

items.label: Identity verification
items.detail: Applies to all members

items.label: Salaried members rule
items.detail: ITA 2007 can treat members as employees

scenes.heading: What This Module Covers
scenes.narration: An LLP wins over a limited company where allocation flexibility matters and members are individuals, as corporate members trigger mixed-membership rules. We'll cover all of this.

scenes.heading: Charity Registration
scenes.subheading: Dual-regulated: the Charity Commission for charity law, HMRC for tax
scenes.narration: Setting up a UK charity is more complex than a limited company, because it answers to two regulators: the Charity Commission, or its Scottish or Northern Irish equivalent, and HMRC for tax.

scenes.heading: Three structural choices
scenes.narration: There are three structures. An unincorporated charity suits very small charities but leaves trustees personally liable. The company limited by guarantee is the classic medium or large form, and the CIO, introduced in 2013, has one regulator.

items.label: Unincorporated charity
items.detail: Trustees personally liable; no separate legal person

items.label: Company ltd by guarantee
items.detail: Registered at Companies House and Charity Commission

items.label: CIO
items.detail: Charity Commission only; Foundation or Association type

scenes.heading: Five setup steps
scenes.narration: Start by defining purposes from the thirteen heads in section 3 of the Charities Act 2011, draft the governing document, appoint fit and proper trustees, then register with the Commission and with HMRC.

items.label: Define purposes
items.detail: From the 13 heads in Charities Act 2011 section 3

items.label: Governing document
items.detail: Trust deed, constitution or articles

items.label: Appoint trustees
items.detail: Typically at least 3, fit and proper

items.label: Register with Commission
items.detail: Via the online portal

items.label: Register with HMRC
items.detail: For tax exemption and Gift Aid

scenes.heading: Key thresholds
scenes.narration: Charities register with the Commission once annual income reaches five thousand pounds, though CIOs register from day one. Income over five hundred thousand pounds means accounts under the Charities SORP.

items.label: Registration threshold
items.detail: Annual income; CIOs register from day one

items.label: Charities SORP accounts
items.detail: Income above this uses SORP under FRS 102

items.label: Audit: gross income
items.detail: Audit required at this level

items.label: Audit: income and assets
items.detail: Assets above this with income of £500k or more

scenes.heading: Accounting framework
scenes.narration: Larger charities with income over five hundred thousand pounds prepare accounts under the Charities SORP, while smaller ones can use simpler receipts and payments accounts.

items.label: Charities SORP, FRS 102
items.detail: For income above £500k

items.label: Receipts and payments
items.detail: For smaller charities

scenes.heading: What this module covers
scenes.narration: In this module we'll walk through choosing the right structure, the mechanics of registration, and the trustees' compliance calendar for year one.

scenes.heading: Sole Trader to Limited Company
scenes.subheading: The most common UK transition, and the most commonly botched
scenes.narration: Moving from sole trader to limited company is the most common transition in the UK, and the most commonly botched. Getting it right saves your client years of tax and compliance pain.

scenes.heading: Done Badly vs Done Well
scenes.narration: Done badly, it can trigger capital gains tax on goodwill and waste loss relief. Done well, it preserves trading losses, secures Business Asset Disposal Relief later, and sets up tax-efficient extraction from day one.

items.label: Done badly
items.detail: CGT on goodwill, stranded VAT, wasted loss relief

items.label: Done well
items.detail: Losses kept, BADR secured, salary, dividends and pension

scenes.heading: The Process: Setting Up
scenes.narration: The nine-step process starts with cessation accounts and valuing goodwill and tangible assets. Then you incorporate, sign the sale agreement for shares plus a director's loan account credit, and transfer trade and staff.

items.label: 1. Cessation accounts
items.detail: Close off the sole trade

items.label: 2. Value the business
